events.enhanced_description: The Polish government officially banned the Solidarity trade union, which had been a significant force for reform and workers' rights in the country. This action followed the suspension of the union in December 1981 and intensified the struggle for democracy in Poland.
events.name: Poland bans the Solidarity trade union

events.enhanced_description: The Mary Rose, the flagship of King Henry VIII, was raised from the Solent after having sunk in 1545. This significant archaeological event provided invaluable insights into Tudor naval history and maritime technology.
events.name: Raising of the Mary Rose

events.enhanced_description: During a UEFA Cup match between FC Spartak Moscow and HFC Haarlem, a tragic disaster occurred at Luzhniki Stadium, resulting in the deaths of 66 people due to a crowd crush. This incident raised serious concerns about crowd control and safety at sporting events.
events.name: Luzhniki disaster

events.enhanced_description: In a significant cultural shift, Dominion Day was officially renamed Canada Day, reflecting the country's evolving identity and independence. This change marked a new era in how Canadians celebrate their national pride.
events.name: Dominion Day renamed Canada Day

events.enhanced_description: The Socialist Party achieved a historic victory in the Spanish general elections, leading to the election of Felipe González as Prime Minister. This marked a significant shift in Spanish politics, moving away from decades of conservative rule.
events.name: Socialist Party wins election in Spain

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic explosion occurred when a gasoline tanker ignited in the Salang Tunnel, resulting in the deaths of at least 176 people. This disaster highlighted the dangers of transportation infrastructure in conflict zones.
events.name: Salang Tunnel explosion

events.enhanced_description: Ahmadou Ahidjo resigned as President of Cameroon, paving the way for Paul Biya to assume leadership. Biya's presidency would extend for over four decades, significantly shaping Cameroon's political landscape.
events.name: Ahmadou Ahidjo resigns as President of Cameroon

events.enhanced_description: Kenan Evren was appointed as the seventh president of Turkey following a constitutional referendum. His presidency was marked by significant political changes and controversies in the wake of the military coup.
events.name: Kenan Evren becomes President of Turkey

events.enhanced_description: A bombing at the Tyre headquarters in Lebanon resulted in the deaths of between 89 and 102 people, exacerbating the ongoing violence in the region. This attack was part of the larger context of the Lebanese Civil War and its associated conflicts.
events.name: Tyre headquarters bombing in Lebanon

events.enhanced_description: Yuri Andropov, the former head of the KGB, was appointed as the General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party's Central Committee, succeeding Leonid Brezhnev. His leadership marked a transitional period in Soviet politics during the Cold War.
events.name: Yuri Andropov becomes General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party

events.enhanced_description: Lech Wałęsa, the leader of Poland's outlawed Solidarity movement, was released from 11 months of internment near the Soviet border. His release was a pivotal moment in the struggle for democracy in Poland.
events.name: Lech Wałęsa released from internment

events.enhanced_description: The General Union of Ecuadorian Workers (UGTE) was founded, aiming to represent the interests of workers in Ecuador. This organization played a crucial role in advocating for labor rights and social justice in the country.
events.name: General Union of Ecuadorian Workers (UGTE) founded

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1982, representatives from 88 countries convened in Geneva to discuss global trade issues and explore pathways toward free trade agreements. This gathering highlighted the growing importance of international cooperation in economic matters during the early 1980s.
events.name: World Trade Conference in Geneva

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1982, Yasuhiro Nakasone was appointed as the Prime Minister of Japan, marking the beginning of a significant political era characterized by economic reforms and a strong alliance with the United States. His leadership would influence Japan's role on the global stage throughout the 1980s.
events.name: Yasuhiro Nakasone becomes Prime Minister of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1982, the Edmonton Eskimos achieved an unprecedented fifth consecutive Grey Cup victory by defeating the Toronto Argonauts 32-16 in the 70th Grey Cup game. This remarkable feat solidified their dominance in Canadian football history.
events.name: Edmonton Eskimos win 70th Grey Cup

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1982, Michael Jackson released his sixth studio album, 'Thriller,' in the United States. The album would go on to become the best-selling album of all time, with over 110 million units sold worldwide, revolutionizing the music industry.
events.name: Michael Jackson releases Thriller

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1982, Miguel de la Madrid was inaugurated as the President of Mexico. His presidency was marked by significant economic challenges and efforts to modernize the country's economy.
events.name: Miguel de la Madrid takes office

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1982, Barney Clark, a 61-year-old retired dentist, became the first person to receive a permanent artificial heart at the University of Utah. He lived for 112 days with the device, marking a significant milestone in medical technology.
events.name: First permanent artificial heart implanted

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1982, the People's Republic of China adopted its current constitution, which laid the groundwork for the country's legal framework and governance structure. This constitution has undergone several amendments since its adoption.
events.name: People's Republic of China adopts constitution

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1982, the first execution by lethal injection in the United States was carried out at the Huntsville Unit in Texas. This method of execution would become a standard practice in many states across the country.
events.name: First U.S. execution by lethal injection

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1982, a series of politically motivated murders occurred in Suriname, known as the December murders. This event was a significant moment in the country's political history, leading to international condemnation.
events.name: December murders in Suriname

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1982, the Swedish pop group ABBA made their final public performance on the British television program 'The Late, Late Breakfast Show.' This performance marked the end of an era for one of the most successful pop groups in history.
events.name: ABBA's final public performance

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1982, a 6.2 magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Yemen, causing severe damage and resulting in approximately 2,800 fatalities. This disaster highlighted the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: North Yemen earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1982, the United Freedom Front carried out bombings targeting offices of South African Airways in Elmont, NY, and IBM in Harrison, NY. These attacks were part of a broader campaign against companies perceived to support apartheid in South Africa.
events.name: United Freedom Front bombings

events.enhanced_description: The Tragedia de Tacoa, occurring on December 19, 1982, was a catastrophic oil tank fire in Venezuela that resulted in significant loss of life and raised awareness about industrial safety standards. The incident underscored the dangers associated with oil production and storage.
events.name: Tragedia de Tacoa

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1982, the Indian Ocean Commission was established by the Port Louis Agreement, aiming to promote regional cooperation and development among Indian Ocean island nations. This organization plays a crucial role in addressing shared challenges in the region.
events.name: Indian Ocean Commission created

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1982, Time magazine named the computer as its Man of the Year, marking the first time a non-human entity received this honor. This decision reflected the growing impact of technology on society and the economy.
events.name: Time magazine's Man of the Year

events.enhanced_description: In January 1983, the migration of the ARPANET to the TCP/IP protocol was officially completed, marking the beginning of the modern Internet. This transition was a pivotal moment in the development of global communications.

image.caption: A logical map of the ARPANET network.
image.credit: ARPANET — The Computer History Museum ( [1] ), en:File:Arpnet-map-march-1977.png
image.date_qualification: Map depicting the ARPANET circa 1977; it predates the January 1983 TCP/IP transition and is contextual, not a depiction of that transition.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: ARPANET migration to TCP/IP completed

events.enhanced_description: During the Assam agitation, the Nellie massacre occurred, resulting in the deaths of over 2,000 people, predominantly Bangladeshi Muslims, highlighting the ethnic tensions and violence in the region.
events.name: Nellie massacre

events.enhanced_description: The bombing of the United States embassy in Beirut resulted in the deaths of 63 people, underscoring the dangers faced by diplomatic missions in conflict zones.

image.caption: Photograph of the U.S. Embassy in Beirut after the bombing.
image.credit: Claude Salhani — Originally from en.wikipedia ; description page is/was here .
image.date_qualification: Depicted date: 21 April 1983; this is an aftermath photograph, not a photograph of the bombing itself. The listed 24 October 2007 date is the original upload date, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: United States embassy bombing in Beirut

events.enhanced_description: The Disney Channel was launched in the United States, marking a significant expansion of Disney's media presence and targeting family-friendly programming.
events.name: Launch of the Disney Channel

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1983, a North Korean Ilyushin Il-62M jet crashed into the Fouta Djallon Mountains in Guinea, resulting in the deaths of all 23 people on board. The incident raised concerns about aviation safety and the geopolitical implications of North Korean flights.
events.name: North Korean Jet Crash in Guinea

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, a technical failure at the Philippsburg Nuclear Power Plant in Germany led to the release of iodine-131, raising alarms about nuclear safety protocols. This incident highlighted the risks associated with nuclear energy during a period of heightened scrutiny.
events.name: Philippsburg Nuclear Power Plant Incident

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, Nintendo launched its Family Computer, also known as the Famicom, in Japan. This gaming console would revolutionize the video game industry and lay the foundation for Nintendo's future success.
events.name: Launch of Nintendo's Family Computer

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, an attack at Orly Airport in Paris resulted in eight deaths and 55 injuries. This incident was part of a series of violent acts linked to political extremism in France during that period.
events.name: Orly Airport Attack

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, heavy rain and subsequent mudslides in western Shimane Prefecture, Japan, resulted in the deaths of 117 people. This disaster underscored the vulnerability of the region to extreme weather events.
events.name: Heavy Rain and Mudslides in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1983, Gulf Air Flight 771 was tragically brought down by a bomb explosion in the baggage compartment shortly after takeoff from Abu Dhabi, resulting in the loss of 117 lives. This incident highlighted the vulnerabilities in aviation security during a time of rising geopolitical tensions in the region.
events.name: Gulf Air Flight 771 crash

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, escalating tensions between native Kanaks and French expatriates in New Caledonia erupted into violence, as the French government retracted its promise of independence for the territory. This conflict marked a significant period of unrest and struggle for self-determination in the region.
events.name: Violence in New Caledonia

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, a mass burial of approximately 700,000 unsold Atari video game cartridges, consoles, and computers took place in Alamogordo, New Mexico. This event became symbolic of the video game crash of 1983, marking a significant downturn in the gaming industry.
events.name: Atari video game burial

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, the Australian yacht Australia II made history by winning the America's Cup, breaking the New York Yacht Club's 132-year hold on the prestigious sailing trophy. This victory was a significant moment for Australia, symbolizing national pride and achievement.
events.name: Australia II wins America's Cup

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, the word processor software Multi-Tool Word, which would later evolve into Microsoft Word, was released in the United States. Developed by Richard Brodie and Charles Simonyi, this software played a pivotal role in the evolution of personal computing and office productivity.
events.name: Release of Multi-Tool Word

events.enhanced_description: In 1983, a bomb exploded in the United States Senate, targeting Republican senators but resulting in no injuries. The attack was carried out by members of the May 19th Communist Organization, reflecting the era's political violence.
events.name: 1983 U.S. Senate bombing

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1983, twenty-five members of the Red Brigades were sentenced to life imprisonment for their involvement in the 1978 murder of Italian politician Aldo Moro. This event underscored the ongoing struggle against political extremism in Italy.
events.name: Red Brigades sentenced for Aldo Moro murder

events.enhanced_description: The Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) was launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base to conduct the world's first all-sky infrared survey from space, significantly advancing the field of infrared astronomy.
events.name: IRAS is launched

events.enhanced_description: The pilot shaft of the Seikan Tunnel, the world's longest sub-aqueous tunnel at 53.85 km, broke through, marking a significant milestone in engineering and transportation in Japan.
events.name: Seikan Tunnel pilot shaft breakthrough

events.enhanced_description: Giovanni Vigliotto went on trial facing charges of polygamy involving 105 women, a case that drew significant media attention and public interest regarding marital laws.
events.name: Giovanni Vigliotto trial

events.enhanced_description: Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser was granted a double dissolution of both houses of parliament, leading to elections on March 5, 1983. This political maneuver resulted in a leadership change within the Australian Labor Party as Bob Hawke succeeded Bill Hayden.
events.name: Double dissolution in Australia

events.enhanced_description: The team of A. J. Foyt, Preston Henn, Bob Wollek, and Claude Ballot-Léna won the prestigious 24 Hours of Daytona automobile race in a Porsche 935, showcasing endurance racing at its finest.
events.name: 24 Hours of Daytona

events.enhanced_description: In Lahore, Pakistan, approximately 100 women protested against military dictator Zia-ul-Haq's proposed Law of Evidence. Despite facing police brutality, including tear gas and baton charges, the protest was successful in repealing the law.
events.name: Women's protest in Lahore

events.enhanced_description: The Ash Wednesday bushfires ravaged parts of Victoria and South Australia, resulting in the tragic loss of 75 lives and marking one of Australia's worst bushfire disasters.
events.name: Ash Wednesday bushfires

events.enhanced_description: The Wah Mee massacre, which took place on February 18, 1983, was a tragic event where multiple individuals were killed in a gambling club in Seattle. This incident highlighted issues related to organized crime and violence in gambling establishments.
events.name: Wah Mee massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Venezuelan bolívar was devalued and exchange controls were established in an event now referred to as Black Friday, marking a significant economic crisis in Venezuela as the bolívar had been one of the most stable currencies.
events.name: Venezuelan bolívar devaluation (Black Friday)

events.enhanced_description: The final episode of the iconic television series M*A*S*H, titled 'Goodbye, Farewell and Amen,' aired on CBS, drawing a record audience of 121.6 million viewers and marking a significant moment in television history.
events.name: Final episode of M*A*S*H

events.enhanced_description: The Balearic Islands and Madrid were officially designated as Autonomous communities of Spain, marking a significant step in the decentralization of political power in the country.
events.name: Autonomous communities of Spain

events.enhanced_description: Chuck Hull invented the 3D printer, revolutionizing manufacturing and design processes by allowing for the creation of three-dimensional objects from digital models.
events.name: Invention of the 3D printer

events.enhanced_description: Yamoussoukro was officially designated as the political capital of Ivory Coast, marking a significant administrative shift from the previous capital, Abidjan.
events.name: Yamoussoukro becomes political capital

events.enhanced_description: The Space Shuttle Challenger was launched on its maiden voyage, STS-6, marking a significant milestone in NASA's space exploration efforts.
events.name: Space Shuttle Challenger STS-6 launch

events.enhanced_description: Spanish golfer Seve Ballesteros won the 47th PGA Masters Tournament, solidifying his status as one of the leading figures in professional golf.
events.name: Seve Ballesteros wins PGA Masters

events.enhanced_description: The bombing of the United States embassy in Beirut resulted in the deaths of 63 people, highlighting the ongoing violence and instability in Lebanon during the civil war.
events.name: 1983 United States embassy bombing in Beirut

events.enhanced_description: A reactor shutdown occurred at the Kursk Nuclear Power Plant due to a failure of fuel rods, raising concerns about nuclear safety in the region.
events.name: Kursk Nuclear Power Plant reactor shutdown

events.enhanced_description: Stern magazine published the so-called 'Hitler Diaries,' which were later revealed to be forgeries, causing a major scandal in journalism and historical scholarship.
events.name: Stern magazine publishes Hitler Diaries

events.enhanced_description: Aberdeen F.C. triumphed over Real Madrid with a score of 2-1 after extra time to win the European Cup Winners' Cup, becoming only the third Scottish side to claim a European trophy.
events.name: Aberdeen F.C. wins European Cup Winners' Cup

events.enhanced_description: Lebanon, Israel, and the United States signed an agreement regarding the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon, a significant step towards stabilizing the region post-civil war.
events.name: Agreement on Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1983, two separate research teams led by Robert Gallo and Luc Montagnier published findings in the journal Science, suggesting the discovery of a novel retrovirus linked to HIV/AIDS. This groundbreaking work laid the foundation for understanding the virus and developing treatments for the disease.
events.name: Declaration of HIV/AIDS Retrovirus Discovery

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1983, Hamburger SV triumphed over Juventus with a score of 1-0 in the final of the European Cup held in Athens. This victory marked a significant achievement for the German club in European football.
events.name: Hamburger SV vs Juventus - European Cup Final

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1983, a powerful 7.8 magnitude earthquake struck northern Honshu, Japan, causing severe shaking and generating a destructive tsunami. The disaster resulted in approximately 100 fatalities and significant damage to infrastructure.
events.name: Sea of Japan Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1983, an explosion at an illegal fireworks operation near Benton, Tennessee, resulted in the tragic deaths of eleven individuals and injuries to one. The blast was powerful enough to be heard from a distance of 20 miles.
events.name: Benton Fireworks Disaster

events.enhanced_description: The 9th G7 Summit commenced on May 28, 1983, in Williamsburg, Virginia, gathering leaders from the world's major industrialized nations to discuss pressing global issues. This summit was part of an ongoing series of meetings aimed at fostering international cooperation.
events.name: 9th G7 Summit

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1983, the Second Sudanese Civil War erupted, marking a significant conflict in Sudan's history. The war was primarily fought between the Sudanese government and various rebel groups, leading to widespread devastation and loss of life.
events.name: Second Sudanese Civil War Begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1983, Britain's Conservative government, led by Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, was re-elected with a landslide majority. This victory solidified Thatcher's position and policies during a tumultuous period in British politics.
events.name: Margaret Thatcher's Conservative Government Re-elected

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1983, Pioneer 10 became the first human-made object to pass the orbit of Neptune, marking a significant milestone in space exploration. This achievement demonstrated the capabilities of human engineering and expanded our understanding of the solar system.
events.name: Pioneer 10 Passes Neptune's Orbit

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1983, 15-year-old Emanuela Orlandi mysteriously disappeared in Vatican City while returning home from a music lesson. Her case has since become one of Italy's most famous mysteries, surrounded by various conspiracy theories and speculations.
events.name: Emanuela Orlandi Disappearance

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1983, India achieved a historic victory over the West Indies in the final of the 1983 Cricket World Cup held at Lord's in London. This win marked India's first World Cup title and a significant moment in cricket history.
events.name: 1983 Cricket World Cup Final

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1983, a total loss of coolant occurred at the Embalse Nuclear Power Station in Argentina, classified as a level 4 incident on the International Nuclear Event Scale. This incident raised concerns about nuclear safety and operational protocols.
events.name: Embalse Nuclear Power Station Incident

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1983, the Polish government announced the end of martial law, which had been in effect since December 1981, and granted amnesty to political prisoners. This marked a significant step towards political reform in Poland, amidst growing pressure from the Solidarity movement and international scrutiny.
events.name: End of Martial Law in Poland

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1983, the lowest natural temperature ever directly recorded at ground level on Earth was measured at Vostok Station in Antarctica, reaching a chilling -128.6 degrees Fahrenheit (-89.2 degrees Celsius). This record has significant implications for climate science and our understanding of extreme weather conditions.
events.name: lowest temperature recorded on Earth

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1983, Australian aviator Dick Smith completed a solo circumnavigation of the globe in a helicopter. This remarkable feat showcased his skills as a pilot and adventurer, inspiring many in the field of aviation.
events.name: Dick Smith's Helicopter Circumnavigation

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1983, 13 soldiers of the Sri Lanka Army were killed in an ambush by the militant group Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), marking a significant escalation in the Sri Lankan Civil War. This incident intensified the conflict that would last until 2009.
events.name: Ambush of Sri Lanka Army Soldiers

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on July 24, 1983, the Black July riots in Sri Lanka led to the deaths of between 400 and 3,000 Tamils, marking a turning point in ethnic tensions in the country. The violence was a response to the earlier ambush of Sri Lankan soldiers and escalated the civil conflict.

image.caption: Tamil Eelam flag associated with the LTTE era.
image.date_qualification: A flag, not a contemporaneous photograph of the Black July riots. The saved image date is 2019-09-12.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Black July Anti-Tamil Riots

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1983, Thomas Sankara became the President of Upper Volta, later renamed Burkina Faso. His leadership was marked by progressive reforms and a strong stance against neocolonialism.
events.name: Thomas Sankara Becomes President

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1983, Hurricane Alicia struck the Texas coast, resulting in 22 fatalities and causing over $3.8 billion in damages. The hurricane was one of the costliest natural disasters in Texas history.
events.name: Hurricane Alicia Hits Texas

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1983, Benigno Aquino Jr., a prominent opposition leader in the Philippines, was assassinated upon his return from exile in the United States. His death sparked widespread protests and was a catalyst for the People Power Revolution.
events.name: Assassination of Benigno Aquino Jr.

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1983, heavy rain triggered severe flooding in Bilbao and surrounding areas, resulting in 44 deaths and causing millions in damages. This disaster highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban areas to extreme weather.
events.name: Flooding in Bilbao, Spain

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1983, Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down by a Soviet Air Force pilot near Moneron Island after the aircraft strayed into Soviet airspace. All 269 passengers and crew members were killed, including U.S. Congressman Larry McDonald, escalating Cold War tensions.
events.name: Korean Air Lines Flight 007 Incident

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1983, the Soviet Union publicly admitted to shooting down Korean Air Lines Flight 007, claiming that the pilots did not recognize it as a civilian aircraft. This admission further strained U.S.-Soviet relations during the Cold War.

image.caption: The Soviet Kashin-class destroyer Odarennyy observes U.S. Seventh Fleet ships during search operations for Korean Air Lines Flight 007.
image.date_qualification: A photograph from the search operations following the September 1, 1983 shootdown; the source says it was photographed in 1983 and published in 1984. The image is not of the September 6 Soviet admission.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Soviet Admission of Shooting Down Flight 007

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1983, Saint Kitts and Nevis became an independent state, marking a significant milestone in the Caribbean's post-colonial history. This independence was part of a broader movement for self-determination in the region.
events.name: Independence of Saint Kitts and Nevis

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1983, Gulf Air Flight 771 crashed in the United Arab Emirates after a bomb exploded in the baggage compartment, killing 117 people. This tragic event raised concerns about aviation security in the region.
events.name: Gulf Air Flight 771 Bombing

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1983, Soviet military officer Stanislav Petrov averted a potential nuclear war by correctly identifying a warning of an incoming missile attack as a false alarm. His decision not to escalate the situation is credited with preventing a catastrophic conflict.
events.name: 1983 Soviet Nuclear False Alarm Incident

events.enhanced_description: In a critical moment on September 26, 1983, Soviet military officer Stanislav Petrov made a pivotal decision to classify a warning of a U.S. missile attack as a false alarm, averting a potential nuclear catastrophe. His actions are credited with preventing what could have escalated into a global nuclear war.

image.caption: Portrait of Stanislav Petrov in the kitchen of his apartment in Fryazino.
image.date_qualification: Portrait made on 2016-07-03, decades after the 1983 incident; it depicts Petrov, not the incident itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Stanislav Petrov nuclear false alarm incident

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1983, the Soyuz T-10-1 mission faced a critical pad abort when a fire broke out at the launch pad. The crew's escape system successfully activated, allowing them to escape just moments before the rocket exploded, showcasing the importance of safety measures in space exploration.
events.name: Soyuz T-10-1 pad abort

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1983, Richard Stallman publicly announced the GNU Project, aimed at creating a free Unix-like operating system. This initiative laid the groundwork for the free software movement and has had a lasting impact on software development.
events.name: Announcement of the GNU Project

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1983, Neil Kinnock was elected as the leader of the British Labour Party, marking a pivotal moment in British politics as he sought to revitalize the party and challenge the Conservative government. His leadership would influence Labour's direction in the years to come.
events.name: Neil Kinnock elected leader of the British Labour Party

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1983, British entrepreneur Richard Noble set a new land speed record of 633.468 mph (1,019.468 km/h) driving the Thrust2 at the Black Rock Desert in Nevada. This achievement showcased advancements in engineering and speed technology.
events.name: Richard Noble sets land speed record

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1983, a bombing in Rangoon killed South Korea's Foreign Minister Lee Bum Suk and 21 others, with North Korean operatives suspected of orchestrating the attack. This incident escalated tensions between North and South Korea during a fraught period in their history.
events.name: Rangoon bombing

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1983, former Japanese Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka was found guilty of accepting a $2 million bribe from Lockheed Corporation and was sentenced to four years in prison. This case was a significant moment in Japan's political landscape, highlighting corruption issues.
events.name: Kakuei Tanaka bribery conviction

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1983, the world's first commercial mobile cellular telephone call was made in Chicago, marking a revolutionary moment in telecommunications. This event paved the way for the mobile communication era that would transform how people connect.
events.name: First commercial mobile phone call

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1983, Maurice Bishop, the Prime Minister of Grenada, was assassinated during a military coup along with 40 others. This event led to significant political upheaval in Grenada and prompted U.S. intervention shortly thereafter.
events.name: Assassination of Maurice Bishop

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1983, at the 17th General Conference on Weights and Measures, the definition of the metre was officially changed to be based on the speed of light, establishing a new standard for measurement that would have lasting implications in science and engineering.

image.caption: Historic Dutch replicas of metric standards in the Rijksmuseum collection, including an iron metre, kilogram, and volume measures.
image.date_qualification: Image photographed 2017-12-17; objects described as dating from 1798, 1799, and 1829. Not an image of the 1983 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Definition of the metre

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1983, simultaneous suicide truck bombings targeted the French Army and U.S. Marine Corps barracks in Beirut, resulting in the deaths of 241 U.S. servicemen, 58 French paratroopers, and 6 Lebanese civilians. This tragic event underscored the volatile nature of the Lebanese Civil War and foreign military involvement.
events.name: Beirut barracks bombing

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1983, U.S. troops invaded Grenada at the request of Dominica's Prime Minister Eugenia Charles, following the assassination of Prime Minister Maurice Bishop. This military intervention was justified by the U.S. as a means to restore order and protect American citizens on the island.
events.name: Invasion of Grenada

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1983, Argentina held its first democratic elections after seven years of military rule, marking a significant turning point in the nation's history. This election was a crucial step towards restoring democracy and addressing the human rights abuses of the previous regime.
events.name: Argentine general election

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1983, South Africa approved a new constitution that granted limited political rights to Coloureds and Asians, representing a controversial step in the apartheid reform process. This move was met with mixed reactions and highlighted the ongoing struggle for equality in the country.
events.name: South Africa's new constitution

events.enhanced_description: The battle of Tripoli commenced on November 3, 1983, between loyalists of Yasser Arafat and dissidents within the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). This conflict was part of the broader struggles for power and influence within Lebanon during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Battle of Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1983, an explosive decompression accident occurred off the coast of Norway involving the Byford Dolphin rig, resulting in the deaths of five divers and severe injuries to another. This tragic incident raised significant concerns about safety protocols in deep-sea diving operations.

image.caption: The Byford Dolphin oil exploration rig in dry dock at Invergordon, Scotland.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2008-02-27, approximately 25 years after the 1983 accident.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Byford Dolphin rig diving bell accident

events.enhanced_description: In November 1983, the NATO exercise Able Archer 83 was conducted, which many Soviet officials misinterpreted as a potential nuclear first strike. This misunderstanding led to heightened tensions and the last significant nuclear scare of the Cold War, emphasizing the fragility of international relations during this period.

image.caption: Memorandum from CIA Director William Casey to President Reagan and other Cabinet-level officials about Soviet military indicators.
image.date_qualification: 1984, as identified in the filename; the image metadata supplies no depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Able Archer 83

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1983, U.S. President Ronald Reagan became the first sitting president to address Japan's National Diet, symbolizing the strengthening of U.S.-Japan relations during a critical period in the Cold War. His speech emphasized cooperation and mutual interests between the two nations.
events.name: Ronald Reagan addresses the National Diet

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1983, the first U.S. cruise missiles arrived at RAF Greenham Common in the UK, sparking widespread protests from peace campaigners. This event was a significant moment in the Cold War, reflecting the tensions surrounding nuclear arms deployment in Europe.

image.caption: Runway at RAF Greenham Common.
image.date_qualification: Late 1980s, as described; the image is not dated to the 13 November 1983 arrival.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Arrival of U.S. cruise missiles in the UK

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1983, the FDA approved the immunosuppressant cyclosporine, revolutionizing the field of transplantation by significantly improving the success rates of organ transplants. This breakthrough marked a major advancement in medical science and patient care.
events.name: FDA approval of cyclosporine

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1983, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus declared independence, a move that was recognized only by Turkey and led to ongoing tensions with the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus. This declaration was part of the broader conflict stemming from the 1974 Turkish invasion of Cyprus, which followed a coup aimed at uniting the island with Greece.
events.name: The Turkish part of Cyprus declares independence

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1983, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) was founded in Chiapas, Mexico, advocating for the rights of indigenous peoples and social justice. The group would later gain international attention during the 1994 uprising, which called for land reform and an end to neoliberal policies.
events.name: The Zapatista Army of National Liberation is founded in Mexico

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1983, an attempted hijacking of Aeroflot Flight 6833 occurred in Tbilisi, Soviet Georgia, resulting in several casualties. The incident highlighted the tensions and security challenges faced by the Soviet Union during its later years.
events.name: Attempted hijacking of Aeroflot Flight 6833

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1983, Colombian Avianca Flight 011 crashed near Barajas Airport in Madrid, Spain, resulting in the deaths of 181 of the 192 people on board. The tragedy raised concerns about aviation safety and led to investigations into the causes of the crash.
events.name: Colombian Avianca Flight 011 crashes near Barajas Airport

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1983, general elections were held in Venezuela, resulting in the opposition party, Democratic Action, winning a majority in both chambers of Congress and the presidency under Jaime Lusinchi. The elections saw a voter turnout of 87.3%, marking a significant political shift in the country.
events.name: General elections in Venezuela

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1983, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) was established in Kathmandu, Nepal, with the aim of promoting sustainable mountain development in the Hindu Kush-Himalayan region. The center was legitimized through an Act of Parliament in Nepal.
events.name: ICIMOD is established

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1983, two Spanish passenger planes collided on a foggy runway at Madrid Airport, resulting in the deaths of 90 people. This tragic incident raised concerns about airport safety protocols and air traffic control.
events.name: Madrid airport collision

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1983, Federal Treasurer Paul Keating announced the floating of the Australian dollar, marking a significant shift in the country's monetary policy. This decision allowed the currency to be determined by market forces rather than a fixed exchange rate, reflecting broader economic reforms under Prime Minister Bob Hawke's government.
events.name: Australian dollar is floated

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1983, military rule in Argentina came to an end with the inauguration of Raúl Alfonsín as President. This marked the restoration of democracy after years of dictatorship and the beginning of a new political era in the country.
events.name: Military rule ends in Argentina

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1983, Turgut Özal of the Motherland Party (ANAP) formed the new government of Turkey, marking the beginning of a civilian regime after years of military rule. This government initiated significant economic and political reforms in the country.

image.caption: Portrait of Turgut Özal, Turkish Prime Minister.
image.credit: European Communities / Christian Lambiotte — European Commission
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1989-05-23, later than the event date 1983-12-13.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Formation of new government in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1983, a fire broke out at the Alcalá 20 nightclub in Madrid, resulting in 83 fatalities and injuring 47 others. The tragedy raised awareness about fire safety regulations in public venues and led to changes in safety protocols.
events.name: Alcalá 20 nightclub fire

events.enhanced_description: The Nervi highway disaster occurred on December 18, 1983, when a deadly traffic collision resulted in numerous fatalities. This tragic event raised awareness about road safety and the importance of traffic regulations.
events.name: Nervi highway disaster

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1983, the Jules Rimet Trophy, awarded to the FIFA World Cup winners, was stolen from the Brazilian Soccer Confederation building in Rio de Janeiro. The trophy has never been recovered, leading to a significant loss in sports history.
events.name: The Jules Rimet Trophy is stolen

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1983, Pope John Paul II visited Rebibbia prison in Rome to forgive Mehmet Ali Ağca, who had attempted to assassinate him in 1981. This act of forgiveness was a significant moment in the Pope's efforts for reconciliation and peace.
events.name: Pope John Paul II visits Rebibbia prison

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1983, two bomb explosions occurred in France: one on a Paris train killed three and injured 19, while the other at Marseille station killed two and injured 34. These attacks highlighted the ongoing issues of terrorism and security in France during this period.
events.name: Bomb explosions in France

events.enhanced_description: The Winterthur events of the early 1980s were characterized by youth riots that reflected broader social tensions in Switzerland. These riots were a response to issues such as unemployment and social inequality, marking a significant moment in Swiss cultural history.
events.name: Winterthur events

events.enhanced_description: In 1984, the Victoria Agreement was signed, establishing the Indian Ocean Commission to promote regional cooperation among the island nations of the Indian Ocean. This agreement aimed to enhance economic and environmental collaboration in the region.
events.name: The Victoria Agreement is signed, institutionalising the Indian Ocean Commission

events.enhanced_description: In 1984, after nine years of construction, the Itaipu Dam, located on the border of Brazil and Paraguay, began generating power. At the time, it was the largest hydroelectric dam in the world, symbolizing a significant achievement in engineering and energy production.
events.name: Itaipu Dam begins generating power

events.enhanced_description: In 1984, Argentinian footballer Diego Maradona was sold by FC Barcelona in Spain to S.S.C. Napoli in Italy for a world record fee of $10.48 million. This transfer marked the beginning of a legendary career for Maradona in Italian football.
events.name: Diego Maradona sold to Napoli

events.enhanced_description: In response to the famine in Ethiopia, Bob Geldof assembled the supergroup Band Aid to record the charity single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?' in London. Released shortly after its recording, the single became a major fundraising effort, raising millions for famine relief and marking a significant moment in music history.
events.name: Band Aid records Do They Know It's Christmas?

events.enhanced_description: After 12 years of military dictatorship, Julio María Sanguinetti was democratically elected as President of Uruguay, marking a pivotal moment in the country's return to democracy. His election signified hope for political reform and stability in a nation recovering from years of authoritarian rule.
events.name: Julio María Sanguinetti elected President of Uruguay

events.enhanced_description: On January 10, 1984, the United States and the Vatican restored full diplomatic relations after a break that lasted over a century. This significant move was part of a broader strategy by both nations to strengthen ties against the backdrop of the Cold War.
events.name: The United States and the Vatican (Holy See) restore full diplomatic relations

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1984, Steve Jobs unveiled the Macintosh personal computer, which was notable for its graphical user interface and mouse. This launch marked a pivotal moment in personal computing, influencing the design and functionality of future computers.
events.name: Steve Jobs launches the Macintosh personal computer in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1984, during the filming of a Pepsi commercial, Michael Jackson's hair caught fire due to a pyrotechnics accident. This incident led to significant changes in safety protocols for performers and highlighted the risks associated with live performances.
events.name: Michael Jackson's hair caught on fire during the making of the Pepsi commercial

events.enhanced_description: The 1984 Sydney bank robbery involved a dramatic hostage situation that captured public attention and highlighted issues of crime and security in urban Australia. The event raised questions about law enforcement responses to such crises.
events.name: 1984 Sydney bank robbery

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1984, John Buster and his team at Harbor-UCLA Medical Center announced the successful birth resulting from the first embryo transfer from one woman to another. This groundbreaking procedure marked a significant advancement in reproductive technology.
events.name: John Buster and the research team at Harbor–UCLA Medical Center announce history's first embryo transfer from one woman to another, resulting in a live birth

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1984, astronauts Bruce McCandless II and Robert L. Stewart conducted the first untethered spacewalk during the STS-41-B mission aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger. This historic event demonstrated the feasibility of free-flying in space.
events.name: Astronauts Bruce McCandless II and Robert L. Stewart make the first untethered space walk

events.enhanced_description: The 1984 Winter Olympics took place in Sarajevo, Yugoslavia, from February 8 to February 19. This event was notable for being the first Winter Olympics held in a socialist country and showcased a range of winter sports.
events.name: The 1984 Winter Olympics are held in Sarajevo, Yugoslavia

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1984, Konstantin Chernenko was appointed General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, following the death of Yuri Andropov. Chernenko's leadership was characterized by a continuation of Andropov's policies amid growing economic challenges.
events.name: Konstantin Chernenko succeeds the late Yuri Andropov as General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1984, President H. M. Ershad of Bangladesh elevated South Sylhet's sub-division to district status, renaming it Moulvibazar. This administrative change aimed to enhance local governance and development.
events.name: President of Bangladesh, H M Ershad upgrades South Sylhet's sub-division status to a district and renames it back to Moulvibazar

events.enhanced_description: In February 1984, the TED (Technology, Entertainment, Design) conference was founded in Monterey, California. This annual event has since become a global platform for sharing innovative ideas and fostering creativity across various fields.
events.name: TED (conference) is founded

events.enhanced_description: On February 29, 1984, Canadian Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau announced his retirement from politics, marking the end of his influential tenure. Trudeau's leadership was characterized by significant social and economic reforms in Canada.
events.name: Canadian prime minister Pierre Trudeau announces his retirement

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1984, Iran accused Iraq of using chemical weapons during the ongoing Iran-Iraq War, leading to widespread condemnation. The United Nations later condemned the use of chemical weapons on March 30, highlighting the humanitarian crisis of the conflict.
events.name: Iran accuses Iraq of using chemical weapons; the United Nations condemns their use on March 30

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1984, the National Union of Mineworkers initiated a strike in the United Kingdom, with tens of thousands of miners protesting against colliery closures. This strike marked the beginning of a year-long conflict that highlighted the struggles of the mining community.
events.name: The National Union of Mineworkers strikes as tens of thousands of miners in the United Kingdom stop working in protest over colliery closures

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1984, William Francis Buckley, the CIA station chief in Beirut, was kidnapped by the Islamic Jihad Organization. His abduction highlighted the dangers faced by intelligence operatives in the volatile Middle East during this period.
events.name: The United States Central Intelligence Agency station chief in Beirut, William Francis Buckley, is kidnapped by the Islamic Jihad Organization

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1984, General Rahimuddin Khan was appointed interim Governor of Sindh, making him the first individual in Pakistan's history to govern two provinces simultaneously. This appointment underscored the military's influence in Pakistani politics.
events.name: General Rahimuddin Khan becomes the first man in Pakistan's history to rule over two of its provinces

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1984, Indian Squadron Leader Rakesh Sharma was launched into space aboard the Soyuz T-11, becoming the first Indian citizen to travel to space. His mission was a significant milestone for India's space program.
events.name: Indian Squadron Leader Rakesh Sharma is launched into space, aboard the Soyuz T-11

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1984, Palestinian gunmen hijacked Israeli bus number 300, taking hostages and prompting a swift response from Israeli special forces. The operation to free the hostages resulted in the deaths of one hostage and two hijackers.
events.name: Palestinian gunmen take Israeli bus number 300 hostage

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1984, India launched Operation Meghdoot, a military operation that aimed to take control of the Siachen Glacier region, which had been a point of contention with Pakistan. This operation marked the beginning of the Siachen conflict.

locations.name: Siachen Glacier, Jammu and Kashmir, India

events.name: India launches Operation Meghdoot

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1984, the first World Youth Day gathering was held in Rome, Italy, initiated by Pope John Paul II. This event aimed to engage young people in the Catholic faith and has since become a global celebration.
events.name: The first World Youth Day gathering is held in Rome, Italy

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1984, over one million people led by Tancredo Neves took to the streets of São Paulo, Brazil, demanding direct presidential elections during the military government. This massive protest was a pivotal moment in the Diretas Já movement, advocating for democracy.
events.name: More than one million people occupy the streets of São Paulo to demand direct presidential elections

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1984, Metropolitan Police officer Yvonne Fletcher was shot and killed during a demonstration outside the Libyan embassy in London. Her death led to an eleven-day siege of the embassy and a significant deterioration in diplomatic relations between the UK and Libya.
events.name: Metropolitan Police officer Yvonne Fletcher was fatally shot during a demonstration outside the Libyan embassy in London

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1984, 'Advance Australia Fair' was officially proclaimed as Australia's national anthem, alongside the adoption of green and gold as the national colors. This decision reflected a growing sense of national identity in Australia.
events.name: Advance Australia Fair is proclaimed as Australia's national anthem

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1984, an X-class solar flare erupted from the Sun, which is classified as one of the most powerful types of solar flares. Such flares can significantly impact Earth's magnetosphere, leading to disruptions in satellite communications and power grids.
events.name: X-class solar flare erupts on the Sun

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1984, Sultan Iskandar of Johor was officially installed as the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, the King of Malaysia, succeeding Sultan Ahmad Shah. This position is rotated among the nine Malay state rulers every five years, symbolizing unity among the states.
events.name: Sultan Iskandar becomes Yang di-Pertuan Agong of Malaysia

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1984, South Africa, Mozambique, and Portugal signed an agreement regarding the supply of electricity from the Cahora Bassa dam, a significant hydroelectric project in Mozambique. This agreement aimed to enhance regional cooperation and energy security.
figures: Representatives of South Africa, Mozambique, and Portugal
events.name: Agreement on electricity supply from Cahora Bassa dam

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1984, the Swedish pop group The Herreys won the Eurovision Song Contest held in Luxembourg City with their hit song "Diggi-Loo Diggi-Ley." This victory marked Sweden's first win in the competition and propelled the song to top-ten hits across several European countries.
events.name: The Herreys' song "Diggi-Loo Diggi-Ley" wins Eurovision

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1984, the Soviet Union announced its decision to boycott the upcoming Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, in response to the United States' boycott of the 1980 Moscow Olympics. This decision reflected the ongoing tensions of the Cold War and significantly impacted the games.
events.name: Soviet Union announces boycott of 1984 Summer Olympics

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1984, a rare astronomical event occurred when Earth passed directly between Mars and the Sun, known as a transit. Such events provide valuable opportunities for astronomers to study the atmospheres and surfaces of celestial bodies.
events.name: Transit of Earth from Mars

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1984, the Louisiana World Exposition, also known as the 1984 World's Fair, opened in New Orleans. This event showcased innovations in technology and culture, drawing millions of visitors and highlighting the city's unique heritage.
events.name: Louisiana World Exposition opens

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1984, a catastrophic explosion occurred at the Severomorsk Naval Base, destroying two-thirds of the missiles stockpiled for the Soviet Northern Fleet. This disaster was deemed the worst naval incident for the Soviet Navy since World War II, resulting in significant loss of life and resources.
events.name: Severomorsk Disaster

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1984, Australia introduced the one-dollar coin as part of its currency system, replacing the one-dollar banknote. This change was part of a broader effort to modernize the currency and reduce costs associated with paper notes.
events.name: One-dollar coin introduced in Australia

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1984, a methane gas explosion at the Abbeystead water treatment works in Lancashire, UK, tragically killed 16 people. This disaster raised significant concerns about safety regulations in industrial operations.
events.name: Methane gas explosion at Abbeystead

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1984, Liverpool FC triumphed over AS Roma in the final of the European Cup, winning 5-2 after a penalty shootout. This match is remembered as one of the most thrilling finals in the history of the tournament.
events.name: Liverpool beats Roma in European Cup final

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1984, the Indian government initiated Operation Blue Star, a military operation aimed at removing Sikh militants from the Golden Temple in Amritsar. This controversial operation led to significant casualties and heightened tensions within the Sikh community.
events.name: Operation Blue Star begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1984, an F5 tornado struck the town of Barneveld, Wisconsin, causing nearly complete destruction. The tornado resulted in nine fatalities, injured nearly 200 people, and caused over $25 million in damages, marking it as one of the most devastating tornadoes in Wisconsin's history.

image.caption: Aerial photograph of Barneveld after an F5 tornado.
image.credit: Rich Rygh — Original Publication: The Baltimore Sun - June 9, 1984 - Page 1 High Quality: https://journaltimes.com/news/state-and-regional/from-the-archives-deadly-tornado-leveled-barneveld-in-1984/collection_8f7ebfc3-79ce-5551-8825-05f83e0910e2.html?mode=nowapp#14
image.date_qualification: Photographed June 9, 1984; the tornado struck June 8, 1984.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: F5 tornado devastates Barneveld

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1984, Cirque du Soleil was founded in Montreal, Canada, by Guy Laliberté and a group of street performers. This innovative circus company would go on to revolutionize the circus arts with its theatrical flair and artistic performances.
events.name: Cirque du Soleil founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1984, 17-year-old Ricky Kasso murdered Gary Lauwers in Northport, New York. This crime contributed to the growing societal panic regarding the association between heavy metal music and satanism during the 1980s.
events.name: Ricky Kasso murders Gary Lauwers

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1984, Virgin Atlantic made its inaugural flight, marking the beginning of Richard Branson's venture into the airline industry. The airline would go on to become known for its innovative services and customer experience.
events.name: Virgin Atlantic inaugural flight

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1984, the Hayim Association was founded by Prof. Rina Zaizov Marx and parents of children with cancer in Israel. The organization aimed to provide support and resources for pediatric oncology patients and their families.
events.name: Hayim Association founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1984, France defeated Spain 2-0 to win the UEFA Euro 1984 tournament. This victory marked a significant achievement for French football, solidifying their status as a powerhouse in European soccer.
events.name: France wins Euro 84

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1984, John Turner was sworn in as the 17th Prime Minister of Canada, succeeding Pierre Trudeau. His term was marked by economic challenges and a brief tenure before being succeeded by Brian Mulroney later that year.
events.name: John Turner becomes Prime Minister of Canada

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1984, Liechtenstein became the last country in Europe to grant women the right to vote. This landmark decision marked a significant step towards gender equality in the nation.
events.name: Liechtenstein grants women the right to vote

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1984, New Zealand Prime Minister Rob Muldoon called a snap election, which resulted in his defeat by opposition Labour leader David Lange. This election marked a significant shift in New Zealand's political landscape.
events.name: New Zealand snap election

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1984, James Huberty entered a McDonald's in San Ysidro, California, and opened fire, killing 21 people and injuring 19 others before being shot by a police sniper. This tragic event highlighted issues of gun violence and mental health in the United States.

locations.name: San Ysidro, San Diego, California, United States

events.name: San Ysidro McDonald's massacre

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1984, cosmonaut Svetlana Savitskaya became the first woman to perform a spacewalk during her mission aboard the Salyut 7 space station. This milestone was a significant achievement in the history of space exploration and women's contributions to science.
events.name: Salyut 7: first woman spacewalk

events.enhanced_description: The 1984 Summer Olympics, held in Los Angeles from July 28 to August 12, marked a significant moment in sports history, showcasing athletic excellence and innovation. The games were notable for the absence of several countries due to a boycott, yet they achieved remarkable commercial success.
events.name: 1984 Summer Olympics

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1984, Australia began the process of deregulating its banking sector, which aimed to increase competition and efficiency within the financial system. This significant policy shift laid the groundwork for modern banking practices in Australia.
events.name: Australian banks deregulation

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1984, the African republic of Upper Volta officially changed its name to Burkina Faso, meaning 'Land of Incorruptible People.' This change was part of a broader effort by President Thomas Sankara to promote national identity and independence.

image.caption: Orthographic map of Burkina Faso.
image.credit: Africa_(orthographic_projection).svg : Martin23230 derivative work: F l a n k e r , derivative work: Flappiefh — Africa_(orthographic_projection).svg
image.date_qualification: Map of Burkina Faso, not a depiction of the 1984 name change. Image date: 2010-03-28.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Upper Volta changes name to Burkina Faso

events.enhanced_description: During the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, a controversial incident occurred in the women's 3,000 meters final when South African runner Zola Budd collided with American Mary Decker, causing both to fall and not finish the race. This moment became one of the most talked-about events of the games.
events.name: Zola Budd and Mary Decker collision

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1984, John DeLorean was acquitted of all charges related to drug trafficking, which had been a high-profile case that captured public attention. His acquittal marked a significant moment in the ongoing narrative surrounding his controversial automotive legacy.
events.name: John DeLorean acquitted

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1984, half a million people gathered in Manila to demonstrate against the regime of President Ferdinand Marcos, reflecting widespread discontent with his authoritarian rule. This event was part of the larger movement that eventually led to the People Power Revolution.
events.name: Demonstration against Ferdinand Marcos

events.enhanced_description: The Milperra massacre on September 2, 1984, was a violent confrontation between rival motorcycle gangs that resulted in multiple deaths and injuries. This incident underscored the dangers of gang violence and its impact on community safety.
events.name: Milperra massacre

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1984, P. W. Botha was inaugurated as the first executive State President of South Africa, marking a significant shift in the country's political landscape during the apartheid era. His presidency was characterized by attempts at reform amidst growing internal and international pressure.

locations.name: Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: P. W. Botha inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1984, Hezbollah carried out a car bombing at the U.S. Embassy annex in Beirut, resulting in the deaths of 24 people. This attack was part of a broader pattern of violence against Western interests in Lebanon during the civil war.
events.name: Hezbollah car-bombs U.S. Embassy annex

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1984, French President François Mitterrand and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl held hands at the Douaumont ossuary, symbolizing reconciliation between France and Germany after decades of conflict. This moment was a powerful gesture of unity and peace in post-war Europe.
events.name: François Mitterrand and Helmut Kohl holding hands in Douaumont

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1984, the United Kingdom and the People's Republic of China signed the initial agreement to return Hong Kong to China in 1997. This agreement marked a significant moment in the history of colonialism and international diplomacy.
events.name: UK and China sign Hong Kong agreement

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1984, Tim Macartney-Snape and Greg Mortimer made history by becoming the first Australians to reach the summit of Mount Everest, the world's highest peak. Their successful ascent was a significant achievement in the realm of mountaineering, showcasing the capabilities of Australian climbers.
events.name: Tim Macartney-Snape and Greg Mortimer reach the summit of Mount Everest

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1984, Marc Garneau became the first Canadian to travel into space aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger during the STS-41-G mission. This milestone marked a significant achievement for Canada in the field of space exploration.
events.name: STS-41-G: Marc Garneau becomes the first Canadian in space

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1984, the beloved children's television series 'Thomas the Tank Engine & Friends,' created by Britt Allcroft, aired its first two episodes in the United Kingdom. The show quickly became a cultural phenomenon, captivating young audiences with its charming stories and characters.
events.name: Thomas the Tank Engine & Friends broadcasts its first episodes

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1984, astronaut Kathryn D. Sullivan made history as the first American woman to perform a space walk during the STS-41-G mission aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger. This groundbreaking event marked a significant milestone for women in space exploration.
events.name: Kathryn D. Sullivan performs first American space walk

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1984, the Provisional Irish Republican Army (PIRA) carried out a bombing at the Grand Hotel in Brighton, targeting British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and her Cabinet. The attack resulted in five fatalities and numerous injuries, highlighting the ongoing conflict in Northern Ireland.
events.name: Brighton hotel bombing

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1984, the Detroit Tigers triumphed over the San Diego Padres in game five of the World Series, securing the franchise's fourth championship title. This victory was celebrated by fans and marked a significant moment in the history of Major League Baseball.
events.name: Detroit Tigers win World Series

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1984, Jerzy Popiełuszko, a Catholic priest known for his support of the Solidarity movement in Poland, was kidnapped by the secret police. His body was discovered 11 days later, igniting public outrage and highlighting the oppressive tactics of the communist regime.
events.name: Kidnapping of Jerzy Popiełuszko

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1984, the Monterey Bay Aquarium opened its doors to the public after seven years of development and construction. This aquarium has since become a leading institution in marine conservation and education.
events.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium opens

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1984, BBC News, presented by Michael Buerk, aired reports on the devastating famine in Ethiopia, revealing the dire situation where thousands had already died and millions more were at risk. This coverage played a crucial role in raising international awareness and humanitarian response.
events.name: BBC reports on Ethiopian famine

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1984, the European Economic Community announced the allocation of £1.8 million to assist in combating the famine in Ethiopia. This financial aid was part of a broader international effort to address the humanitarian crisis.
events.name: European Economic Community aids Ethiopian famine

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1984, the science fiction action film 'The Terminator,' directed by James Cameron and starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, premiered in Los Angeles. The film became a cultural icon and significantly influenced the science fiction genre.
events.name: The Terminator premieres

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1984, Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her two Sikh bodyguards in New Delhi. This event triggered widespread anti-Sikh riots, resulting in the deaths of thousands and leading to Rajiv Gandhi's ascension as Prime Minister.
events.name: Assassination of Indira Gandhi

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1984, following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, widespread anti-Sikh violence erupted in Delhi and other parts of India. This tragic event resulted in the deaths of an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 Sikhs, marking a dark chapter in Indian history.
events.name: Anti-Sikh mass murder following Indira Gandhi's assassination

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1984, the Sandinista Front won the Nicaraguan general elections, solidifying their control over the country amidst ongoing political turmoil. This victory was significant in the context of the Cold War and U.S. involvement in Central America.
events.name: Sandinista Front wins Nicaraguan elections

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1984, Republican President Ronald Reagan was re-elected, defeating Democratic challenger Walter Mondale with 59% of the popular vote. This election marked one of the largest electoral victories in U.S. history, with Reagan winning 49 out of 50 states.
events.name: 1984 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1984, the first Hackers Conference was held in San Francisco, bringing together computer enthusiasts and pioneers to discuss the emerging field of hacking and technology. This event played a crucial role in shaping the future of computer culture.
events.name: First Hackers Conference held

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1984, the Louisiana World Exposition, also known as the 1984 World's Fair, closed its doors after showcasing innovations and cultural exhibits from around the world. The fair was a significant event for New Orleans, attracting millions of visitors.
events.name: Louisiana World Exposition closes

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1984, Morocco withdrew from the Organization of African Unity in protest against the admission of Western Sahara as a member. This decision underscored the ongoing tensions surrounding the Western Sahara conflict.
events.name: Morocco leaves Organization of African Unity

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1984, Zamboanga City mayor Cesar Climaco, a vocal critic of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, was assassinated in his home city. His death was a significant event in the political landscape of the Philippines during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Assassination of Cesar Climaco

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1984, a series of catastrophic explosions at the Pemex Petroleum Storage Facility in San Juan Ixhuatepec, Mexico City, resulted in a major fire that claimed the lives of approximately 500 people. This disaster highlighted significant safety issues within the petroleum industry.
events.name: Pemex Petroleum Storage Facility explosion

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1984, Operation Moses commenced, facilitating the evacuation of Ethiopian Jews (Beta Israel) from Sudan to Israel. This operation was a significant humanitarian effort during a time of crisis for the Ethiopian Jewish community.
events.name: Start of Operation Moses

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1984, the charity supergroup Band Aid, organized by Bob Geldof, recorded the single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?' in London to raise funds for famine relief in Ethiopia. The song became a global hit and raised significant awareness for the humanitarian crisis.
events.name: Band Aid records charity single

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1984, William Penn and his wife Hannah Callowhill Penn were posthumously granted honorary citizenship of the United States, recognizing their contributions to the founding of Pennsylvania and their legacy in American history.
events.name: Honorary citizenship for William Penn and Hannah Callowhill Penn

events.enhanced_description: The Kent and Dollar Farm massacres mark a significant escalation in the violence of the Sri Lankan Civil War, where the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) initiated a series of attacks against the Sinhalese population, resulting in the deaths of 127 individuals. This event highlighted the deepening ethnic tensions and the brutal nature of the conflict that would continue for decades.
events.name: Kent and Dollar Farm massacres

events.enhanced_description: The Manal Aru massacres in December 1984 involved the killing of Tamil civilians by the Sri Lankan military during the ongoing civil conflict. This tragic event highlighted the severe humanitarian issues arising from the war.
events.name: 1984 Manal Aru massacres

events.enhanced_description: In Cairo, a peace agreement was signed between Kenya and Somalia, where Somalia officially renounced its historical territorial claims. This agreement was a significant step towards improving diplomatic relations between the two nations, which had been strained for decades.
events.name: Peace agreement between Kenya and Somalia

events.enhanced_description: The Cheddikulam massacre on December 2, 1984, was part of a series of violent incidents during the Sri Lankan Civil War, where Tamil civilians were targeted. This event exemplified the brutal realities of the conflict and its devastating impact on civilian populations.
events.name: Cheddikulam massacre

events.enhanced_description: The 1984 Australian federal election resulted in the re-election of Bob Hawke's Labor government, albeit with a reduced majority, defeating the Liberal/National Coalition led by Andrew Peacock. This election was pivotal in shaping the political landscape of Australia during the 1980s.
events.name: 1984 Australian federal election

events.enhanced_description: The Bhopal disaster occurred when a methyl isocyanate leak from a Union Carbide pesticide plant resulted in the immediate deaths of over 8,000 people and injured more than half a million. This catastrophic industrial accident is considered one of the worst in history, with long-lasting effects on the community and environment.
events.name: Bhopal disaster

events.enhanced_description: During the Sri Lankan Civil War, the 1984 Mannar massacre saw Sri Lankan Army soldiers kill over 200 civilians in the town of Mannar. This tragic event underscored the severe human rights violations occurring during the conflict and the ongoing ethnic strife in the region.
events.name: 1984 Mannar massacre

events.enhanced_description: The Kokkilai massacres, occurring on December 16, 1984, involved the Sri Lankan Army's attack on Tamil civilians, further exacerbating the humanitarian crisis during the civil war. These events drew international attention to the ongoing conflict and its toll on innocent lives.
events.name: 1984 Kokkilai massacres

events.enhanced_description: The Sino-British Joint Declaration was signed between the People's Republic of China and the United Kingdom, outlining the future of Hong Kong following its handover in 1997. This agreement established the principle of 'one country, two systems,' which aimed to maintain Hong Kong's autonomy and way of life.
events.name: Sino-British Joint Declaration

events.enhanced_description: The disappearance of Jonelle Matthews from Greeley, Colorado, captured national attention and became a significant case in the discussion of child safety and crime. Her remains were discovered in 2019, leading to further investigations into her tragic fate.
events.name: Disappearance of Jonelle Matthews

events.enhanced_description: In a controversial incident, four African-American youths boarded an express train in the Bronx and demanded money from Bernhard Goetz, who responded by shooting them. This event sparked a national debate about urban crime, racial tensions, and self-defense laws in the United States.
events.name: Bernhard Goetz shooting incident

events.enhanced_description: The Lake Inari missile incident occurred when a Soviet cruise missile accidentally plunged into Lake Inari in Finnish Lapland. This event raised concerns about military safety and international relations during the Cold War, with Finnish authorities announcing the incident publicly shortly after.
events.name: Lake Inari missile incident

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev was appointed General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party, becoming the de facto leader of the Soviet Union. His leadership marked the beginning of significant reforms in the Soviet Union, including policies of glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring).
events.name: Mikhail Gorbachev becomes General Secretary

events.enhanced_description: In 1985, Mohamed Al-Fayed purchased the iconic London department store Harrods, a move that would significantly impact the retail landscape in the UK. Under his ownership, Harrods became synonymous with luxury shopping and high-profile clientele.
events.name: Mohamed Al-Fayed buys Harrods

events.enhanced_description: The Organization Commune Africaine et Malgache was officially dissolved in 1985, marking the end of a regional organization aimed at promoting cooperation among African and Malagasy nations. This dissolution reflected the changing political landscape in Africa during the 1980s.
